title: AI in Classrooms
resolution: Resolved: High schools should allow students to use generative artificial intelligence tools for schoolwork.
summary: Most teens now use chatbots for schoolwork, with or without permission. Should schools allow it, and teach students to use it well, or restrict it?

background.p: Pew Research Center found the share of U.S. teens (13–17) who had used ChatGPT for schoolwork doubled from 13% in 2023 to 26% in 2024; teens were far more likely to call it acceptable for researching new topics (54%) than for writing essays (18%). A fall 2025 Pew survey found about 54% of teens used chatbots for schoolwork, and 59% said cheating with these tools had become a regular part of student life.

Early experiments point both ways. In a randomized trial in a Harvard introductory physics course (Kestin and colleagues, 2025), students learned more from a carefully designed tutoring tool than from an in-class active-learning lesson on the same topic. In a randomized trial with nearly 1,000 high school math students in Turkey (Bastani and colleagues, PNAS 2025), students with an unrestricted chatbot did better during practice but 17% worse on a later exam without it, while students using a version built to give hints rather than answers did about as well as students without the tool.

The difference between the two studies points to the real question: not only *whether* students use these tools, but *how*. Schools' policies range from bans to rules that allow specific uses (brainstorming, feedback, practice) while forbidding others (submitting generated work as one's own).

disputed.q: Do these tools help or hurt learning?
positions: Some controlled studies find well-designed tutoring tools raise learning, sometimes substantially.
Others find unrestricted use acts as a crutch: students do better while using the tool and worse without it.

terms.def: Software that produces text, images or other content in response to prompts, such as chatbots.
Design limits on a tool, such as giving hints instead of full answers.
Honesty in schoolwork: doing your own work and crediting sources.

aff.label: Affirmative
aff.stance: Schools should allow these tools and teach students to use them well, because students will use them anyway and can learn more with them.

args.warrant: A tutor that explains step by step, answers questions instantly and adapts to each student offers help that a teacher with thirty students can't always give.
args.evidence: Kestin and colleagues (2025, Scientific Reports): students learned more with a structured tutoring tool than in an active-learning class session.
args.response: The negative answers that the same evidence shows design matters: unrestricted tools can harm learning, as Bastani and colleagues found.

args.claim: Students already use them; schools should teach responsible use.
args.warrant: Bans push use out of sight. Allowing use with clear rules lets teachers teach when it helps, when it doesn't, and how to check its errors.
args.evidence: Pew surveys showing most teens use chatbots for schoolwork; school district policies that permit specific uses.
args.response: The negative replies that widespread misuse is a reason to restrict, not to permit, and that rules for responsible use are hard to enforce.

args.claim: It helps students who lack other help.
args.warrant: Students whose families can't pay tutors or help with homework gain access to explanations at any hour, narrowing gaps.
args.evidence: Studies of tutoring's effects on achievement; reports on access to private tutoring by family income.
args.response: The negative argues that students with less support may also be most likely to lean on the tool as a crutch.

args.claim: Using these tools is a skill students will need.
args.warrant: Many jobs and colleges now expect people to use these tools; learning to use them critically is part of preparing for that.
args.evidence: Employer surveys; college policies allowing guided use.
args.response: The negative replies that students need strong basic skills first, and the tools change so fast that specific skills date quickly.

neg.label: Negative
neg.stance: Schools should restrict these tools for schoolwork, because they let students skip the thinking that learning requires.

args.warrant: Learning comes from struggling through problems. If a tool supplies answers, students practice copying, not thinking.
args.evidence: Bastani and colleagues (PNAS 2025): students with an unrestricted chatbot scored 17% lower on a later exam without it.
args.response: The affirmative answers that the same study found a hint-based version didn't harm learning, so the answer is rules about design and use, not restriction.

args.claim: It makes cheating easy and hard to detect.
args.warrant: Generated essays and answers are hard to tell apart from student work, which undermines grades and trust.
args.evidence: Pew (2025): 59% of teens say cheating with these tools is a regular part of student life; research on the unreliability of detection software.
args.response: The affirmative replies that cheating happens under bans too; changing assignments (in-class writing, oral checks) works better than prohibition.

args.claim: The tools make mistakes students can't catch.
args.warrant: Chatbots can produce confident but wrong answers. Students who are still learning a subject are the least able to notice.
args.evidence: The Bastani study's finding that the unrestricted tool's answers were correct only about half the time; reports of fabricated citations.
args.response: The affirmative argues that teaching students to check answers is itself valuable, and newer tools with guardrails make fewer errors.

args.warrant: Students' questions and work are sent to private companies, and not every family can afford the best versions.
args.evidence: Student-privacy laws such as FERPA and COPPA; school district reviews of vendor contracts.
args.response: The affirmative replies that schools can choose approved tools with privacy protections and provide them free to all students.

strawmen.strawman: They want students to let a chatbot do all their homework.
strawmen.why: Supporters favor allowed uses with rules, not handing over the work.
strawmen.steelman: Students already use these tools; schools that permit specific uses can teach responsible habits and use well-designed tutors that research shows can raise learning.

strawmen.strawman: They're just afraid of new technology.
strawmen.why: Opponents point to controlled evidence that unrestricted use harms learning, plus cheating and accuracy problems.
strawmen.steelman: Learning requires doing the thinking; unrestricted tools let students skip it, as experiments show, and they make cheating easy and errors hard to catch.

weak.why: They make frequent errors; claiming otherwise is easily refuted.
Overgeneralized; calculators, libraries and the internet have mixed and often positive effects.

aff: What happened in the Bastani study when students used an unrestricted chatbot?
How would a teacher know whether a student wrote an essay?
neg: What did the Harvard physics study find?
If most students already use these tools, does a ban work?
Would you allow a hint-only tutoring tool?
